demand.name: Demand
demand.simple: Someone has to eat the cake. Demand is the consumers and companies who pay for AI. If they stop paying, every layer below feels it.
demand.analyst: Track paid usage, not pilots. The test is whether AI revenue grows faster than AI capex. Watch enterprise renewal rates, seat expansion, token volumes, and consumer subscription churn.
metrics: AI revenue run-rates disclosed by hyperscalers

facts.text: Microsoft said its AI business passed a $37B annual revenue run-rate, up 123% year over year.
Google Cloud backlog nearly doubled in a quarter to over $460B.
Amazon said its backlog stood at $496B, growing triple digits year over year; AWS revenue was $42.2B, up 36.7%.
Google Cloud backlog reached $514B at the end of June 2026, up more than $50B in a quarter.
TSMC Q3 2026 revenue was $46.7B, up 41% in dollars, at a 66.4% gross margin; it guided Q4 to $52.3-54.3B.
ASML booked record Q3 sales of EUR 11.7B and said planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet customer demand.

layers.name: Energy
layers.simple: AI runs on electricity, and lots of it. No power, no AI. Energy is now the slowest and hardest layer to grow.
layers.analyst: Huang calls energy the binding constraint on how much intelligence the system can produce. Interconnection queues, transformer lead times, and gas turbine backlogs set the pace of data center delivery more than chip supply does.
layers.money: Utilities earn a regulated return on what they build (rate base). Independent power producers sell power on long contracts (PPAs) to tech companies, often 10 to 20 years. Equipment makers sell turbines, transformers, and switchgear with multi-year backlogs.
chokepoints: Large power transformers and gas turbines
metrics: Utility capex plans and rate cases
layers.us_china: China has roughly twice the US electricity generation capacity and builds grid faster. Huang flagged this energy gap at CSIS as the main US vulnerability.
layers.bull: Power is the scarcest input, so whoever owns firm power has pricing leverage for a decade.
layers.bear: Regulated utilities cannot capture scarcity pricing. If demand forecasts prove inflated, utilities and ratepayers are left with stranded assets.
exit_rules: Data center PPA signings fall two quarters in a row
A major utility cuts its load-growth forecast
Hyperscalers start cancelling or deferring interconnection requests

layers.name: Chips
layers.simple: Chips do the math. A few companies design them, one company (TSMC) makes most of the best ones, and one company (ASML) makes the machines that make them.
layers.analyst: NVIDIA's moat is CUDA and full-system integration (networking, racks), not only silicon. The share shift to watch is inference: custom chips (Google TPU, Amazon Trainium, Broadcom-designed ASICs) and inference specialists (Cerebras) compete on cost per token.
layers.money: Designers sell chips and systems at very high gross margins. The foundry earns on capacity with huge capex. Equipment makers sell tools with long backlogs. Memory makers (HBM) earn cyclical but currently tight-supply margins.
chokepoints: TSMC advanced nodes and advanced packaging (CoWoS)
metrics: NVIDIA data center revenue and backlog
layers.us_china: The US leads in design and tools, but production sits in Taiwan. China is building domestic chips (Huawei Ascend) under export controls, at lower performance but rising volume.
layers.bull: Every new data center starts with a chip order. Hyperscaler capex guidance is effectively NVIDIA's order book.
layers.bear: Inference economics favor cheaper custom silicon, which compresses NVIDIA's margin. Chips also become obsolete fast, so buyers may slow purchases.
exit_rules: Hyperscaler capex guidance cut by any of the big four
NVIDIA gross margin falls more than 5 points
GPU rental prices drop sharply for current-generation chips

layers.name: Infrastructure
layers.simple: Data centers: giant warehouses full of chips, cooling, cables, and power hookups. Companies rent time on these computers.
layers.analyst: The clouds (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) and neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius) turn capex into rentable compute. This layer carries the depreciation risk: GPUs may be economically obsolete before they are fully depreciated, which can flatter reported earnings.
layers.money: Rent compute by the GPU-hour or under multi-year capacity contracts. Data center owners sign long leases with hyperscalers. Builders and equipment suppliers (cooling, power distribution) earn on construction.
layers.us_china: US hyperscalers dominate global cloud. China's clouds (Alibaba, Tencent, Huawei) build out with domestic chips and cheaper power.
layers.bull: Microsoft says it stays capacity-constrained even at record spend. Backlogs are huge and contracted.
layers.bear: Free cash flow is shrinking as capex soars. Neoclouds carry heavy debt. If demand pauses, this layer absorbs the losses.
exit_rules: Any big-four hyperscaler guides capex down
Cloud revenue growth decelerates for two quarters
Neocloud refinancing at sharply wider spreads

facts.text: Big four 2026 capex plans total about $725B, up 77% from $410B in 2025 (FT tally).
About two-thirds of Microsoft's capex in one recent quarter went to short-lived assets, mainly GPUs and CPUs.
CoreWeave's debt totaled $35.1B at the end of Q1 2026; interest was $536M that quarter.

layers.name: Models
layers.simple: The AI itself. Companies spend billions training a model once, then earn money every time someone uses it.
layers.analyst: Training is a fixed cost; inference is a variable cost that scales with usage. Price per token keeps falling, which is the commoditization risk. Open-weight models (many from China) set a price floor near cost.
layers.money: Consumer subscriptions, per-token API fees, and enterprise licenses. Most frontier labs are private, so public exposure is indirect through hyperscaler stakes.
metrics: Lab revenue run-rates and funding rounds
Open vs closed model performance gap
layers.us_china: US labs lead at the frontier. Chinese open-weight models (DeepSeek, Qwen) lead in open-source adoption and pressure prices globally.
layers.bull: Models crossed a usefulness threshold; usage is compounding and the best labs gain pricing power through enterprise lock-in.
layers.bear: Models flatten into utilities. Falling token prices transfer value to users and app builders, not to labs.
exit_rules: Token prices fall faster than usage grows for two quarters
A frontier lab misses a funding round or takes a down round
Open models match frontier performance on key benchmarks

layers.name: Applications
layers.simple: The tools people actually use: coding helpers, legal assistants, search, self-driving cars. This is where AI has to earn its keep.
layers.analyst: Value capture depends on workflow ownership and proprietary data. Incumbents (Microsoft, Salesforce, ServiceNow) bundle AI into existing seats; AI-native apps (Cursor, Harvey) win on speed. Watch whether pricing moves from per-seat to per-outcome.
layers.money: Per-seat subscriptions, usage-based pricing, or per-outcome fees. Ad-supported consumer apps monetize through better targeting.
chokepoints: Inference cost relative to price charged
metrics: Seats converting from pilot to paid
layers.us_china: US leads in enterprise software. China leads in consumer super-app integration and robotics deployment.
layers.bull: Applications began generating real economic value, and they pull demand through every layer beneath.
layers.bear: AI can undercut seat-based software pricing. Much of the value goes to customers as lower prices rather than vendor profit.
exit_rules: Net revenue retention falls below 110% at key holdings
Seat counts shrink at incumbents as AI replaces users
Inference costs push gross margins down

plate.name: Capital
plate.simple: The money that pays for everything above: company cash flow, bonds, private equity, private credit.
plate.analyst: Funding is shifting from hyperscaler cash flow to off-balance-sheet leases, joint ventures, and private credit. Risk moves to pension funds, insurers, and retail vehicles.

plate.name: Data
plate.simple: What AI learns from. The good public data is used up, so companies now license or create their own.
plate.analyst: Proprietary and licensed data, synthetic data, and user feedback loops are emerging moats. Copyright litigation is the swing factor.

plate.name: Talent
plate.simple: A few thousand top researchers who know how to build frontier AI. They are paid like star athletes.
plate.analyst: Acqui-hires and compensation packages in the hundreds of millions signal scarcity. Talent mobility spreads know-how quickly, which erodes model moats.

plate.name: Policy
plate.simple: The rules: who can sell chips to whom, how fast power plants get approved, who owns training data.
plate.analyst: Export controls, permitting reform, energy regulation, copyright rulings, and state AI laws. Policy can reprice a layer overnight.

plate.name: Materials
plate.simple: Raw stuff: copper for wires, gallium and rare earths for chips and magnets, ultra-pure silicon.
plate.analyst: China dominates refining for many critical minerals and has used export restrictions as leverage. Copper supply is a long-cycle constraint on grid buildout.

dollar_flow.label: Teaching example. Rough order of magnitude, not measured data.

steps.text: The app or model company keeps about $8 for salaries, research, marketing, and margin.
About $6 pays the cloud for compute time, buildings, cooling, and networking.
About $3.50 of the cloud's cost is really the chips, paid back through depreciation.
About $1 ends up as electricity at the power plant.
The rest services the debt and equity that financed the buildout.

facts.text: 2025 data center M&A: 113 deals, more than $69B total value, a record.
Debt issuance by data center owners and operators nearly doubled, from about $92B in 2024 to $182B in 2025.
Since early 2024, 575 data center M&A deals closed worth $151B; 84% of the value came from private equity.
Meta and Blue Owl closed $27B for the Hyperion campus in Louisiana; Blue Owl funds own 80%. The largest private credit deal on record.
Blackstone's data center portfolio passed $150B owned or under construction; data centers are 27% of BREIT fair value.
SoftBank completed its acquisition of DigitalBridge on September 30, 2026, for about $3.1B.
CoreWeave's $2.75B of 9.75% unsecured notes traded near 81 cents, yielding over 15%; its five-year CDS rose to about 881bp from about 547bp at end-June. S&P rates it in the B category.
CCC-rated junk spreads widened to 12.67 points from 9.04 in early May, while the broad high-yield index stayed near 3.2 points: stress is concentrated in the weakest borrowers.

data_centers.simple: A data center is where layers 1, 2, and 3 meet physically: power comes in, chips sit in racks, and the building rents out the computing.
watch: Share of deals with long-term power contracts

facts.text: Data center deal value in the US and Canada totaled about $160B since 2019, versus about $40B in Asia-Pacific and $24B in Europe.
Private equity firms are holding data center assets longer than the typical five-year exit cycle.

bottleneck.why: Chips were the shortage in 2023 and 2024. Now buildings with GPUs on order wait on grid connections, turbines, and transformers.

cycle.assessment: Late build-out. Big-tech capex guides were raised again after Q2 and TSMC and ASML say demand runs ahead of supply into 2028. But Meta's free cash flow is nearly gone, and in October credit markets began pricing the weakest AI borrowers as distressed (CoreWeave unsecured yields above 15%). Stress is concentrated, not systemic, so far.

analogs.name: Railroads, 1840s Britain
analogs.lesson: Real, transformative network; investors still lost heavily when capacity outran traffic.

analogs.name: Telecom fiber, 1999 to 2001
analogs.lesson: Fiber laid in the boom was used for decades, but most builders went bankrupt. Vendor financing inflated demand.

analogs.name: US shale, 2014 to 2016
analogs.lesson: Cheap credit funded growth past demand; a price drop exposed weak balance sheets fast.

scenarios.name: Power shortage
scenarios.desc: Grid connections for new data centers are delayed 2 more years across major US markets.
scenarios.why: Owners of firm power gain pricing power. Chip orders slip because buildings cannot be energized. Existing powered data centers rise in value, offsetting delayed new builds. Model training timelines slip.

scenarios.name: Chip export ban tightens
scenarios.desc: The US bans sales of a broader range of AI chips to China and more countries.
scenarios.why: US chip designers lose revenue; China accelerates domestic chips. Other layers see little near-term change outside China.

scenarios.name: Models get 10x cheaper
scenarios.desc: A breakthrough cuts the compute needed per answer by 90%.
scenarios.why: Short term, the bottom layers lose because less compute is needed per task and model prices fall. Applications gain margin. If usage explodes (Jevons paradox), the bottom layers can recover, but it is not guaranteed.

scenarios.name: Hyperscaler pauses capex
scenarios.desc: One of the big four cuts next-year capex guidance by 25%.
scenarios.why: Capex guidance is the order book for chips and construction. Private credit and data center lenders reprice quickly because loans were underwritten on guidance continuing.

scenarios.name: Enterprise adoption surges
scenarios.desc: AI agents prove reliable; enterprise AI spending doubles in a year.
scenarios.why: Demand pulls on every layer beneath it, all the way to the power plant. The bottleneck shifts further toward energy.

questions.q: In Huang's framework, which layer is the foundation of the cake?
questions.why: Huang puts energy at the base and calls it the binding constraint on how much intelligence the system can produce.

questions.q: Why is energy now the hardest layer to grow quickly?
options: Electricity prices are capped by law
Grid connections, transformers, and turbines take years to deliver
Data centers use less power each year
Utilities refuse to sell to tech companies
questions.why: The constraint is physical lead time: interconnection queues and equipment backlogs run for years, while chips can ship in months.

questions.q: A regulated utility signs a big data center load. How does it mainly earn more money?
options: Earning an allowed return on the new grid assets it builds
Selling GPUs to the data center
questions.why: Regulated utilities earn on rate base. Scarcity pricing goes to unregulated independent power producers like Vistra or Constellation.

questions.q: Which company is closest to a pure play on unregulated power sold to data centers?
questions.why: Constellation is an independent power producer with a large nuclear fleet and data center contracts. Duke is regulated; Equinix is real estate; Broadcom is chips.

questions.q: If transformer lead times double, which asset gains the most value?
options: Data centers already connected to power
questions.why: Scarcity of time-to-power makes already-energized capacity more valuable. Unpowered land loses value relative to it.

questions.q: Which company manufactures most of the world's leading-edge AI chips?
questions.why: NVIDIA designs; TSMC manufactures. ASML makes the lithography machines TSMC uses.

questions.q: What is usually cited as NVIDIA's deepest moat?
questions.why: Developers build on CUDA, and NVIDIA sells whole systems with networking. Switching costs live in software and integration, not just the silicon.

questions.q: Google runs more AI on its own TPUs instead of buying GPUs. Who benefits most?
questions.why: Custom ASICs are often co-designed with Broadcom or Marvell. The shift takes share from merchant GPUs.

questions.q: Why does the shift from training to inference matter for chip winners?
options: Inference rewards cost per token, which opens room for cheaper custom chips
questions.why: Training rewards peak performance; inference at scale rewards efficiency, where custom silicon and specialists compete.

questions.q: Which company is the sole supplier of EUV lithography machines?
questions.why: ASML is the only EUV supplier, a true chokepoint under the whole chip layer.

questions.q: About how much did the big four plan to spend on capex in 2026 (FT tally)?
questions.why: About $725B, up 77% from $410B in 2025. $410B was the 2025 total.

questions.q: Why can long GPU depreciation schedules overstate profits?
options: If chips are useful for 2 to 3 years but depreciated over 5 to 6, annual expense is understated
questions.why: Spreading cost over more years than the asset is useful lowers reported expense now and pushes the hit later.

questions.q: What is a neocloud?
options: A GPU-focused cloud that rents AI compute, like CoreWeave or Nebius
questions.why: Neoclouds specialize in renting GPU capacity, often funded heavily with debt.

questions.q: Which statistic best signals strain beneath record capex?
options: Shrinking free cash flow while capex climbs
questions.why: When capex outpaces operating cash flow, funding shifts to debt and outside capital, which is where cycles break.

questions.q: Meta raised capex guidance and its stock fell about 9%. What does that reaction suggest?
options: Investors are starting to question returns on the spending
Capex is irrelevant to stock prices
questions.why: Revenue beat expectations, yet the stock fell on higher spending. The market began demanding proof of return.

questions.q: How do model companies mostly charge developers?
questions.why: API pricing is per token of input and output; consumers usually pay subscriptions.

questions.q: Why are open-weight models a threat to model-layer profits?
options: They set a near-cost price floor that closed models must compete against
questions.why: Free or cheap capable models cap what anyone can charge for similar quality.

questions.q: You want public-market exposure to frontier labs. Which is the most direct path?
options: Owning hyperscalers with lab stakes (MSFT, AMZN, GOOGL) or SoftBank
questions.why: Most frontier labs are private; exposure runs through strategic investors.

questions.q: Training cost is fixed per model; inference cost scales with use. What does that imply as usage grows?
options: Margins can widen if price per token falls slower than cost per token
questions.why: The economics hinge on the gap between token price and token cost at scale.

questions.q: Where in the cake does Huang say economic benefit finally shows up?
questions.why: Applications convert compute into economic value, and they pull on every layer beneath.

questions.q: Why could AI hurt some software incumbents even as it helps them?
options: If AI replaces users, per-seat revenue shrinks
AI raises their costs to zero
questions.why: Seat-based pricing assumes a human per license. Agents that do the work can shrink seat counts.

questions.q: Which moat is strongest at the application layer?
options: Owning the workflow and proprietary data
questions.why: Models are interchangeable; workflow position and data are hard to copy.

questions.q: In the Meta Hyperion deal, who owns 80% of the campus?
questions.why: Blue Owl funds own 80%; Meta keeps 20% and stays the tenant, keeping debt off its balance sheet.

questions.q: Why do hyperscalers use JVs and private credit instead of borrowing directly?
options: It is cheaper in all cases
It keeps large obligations off their balance sheets and protects credit ratings
Banks refuse to lend to them
questions.why: Off-balance-sheet structures let them build without visibly levering up, while risk shifts to lenders.

questions.q: Which public tickers give the closest daily read on private credit stress?
questions.why: BDCs hold private loans and trade publicly; discounts to net asset value signal stress.

questions.q: Since early 2024, what share of data center M&A value came from private equity (Synergy)?
questions.why: 84% of $151B across 575 deals, showing how dependent the buildout is on outside capital.

questions.q: If a hyperscaler cuts capex guidance, which reprices fastest?
options: Private credit and data center debt underwritten on guidance
questions.why: Much recent debt was priced as if guidance were certain. A cut forces an abrupt reprice.

questions.q: Who acquired DigitalBridge, completing the deal on September 30, 2026?
questions.why: SoftBank completed the roughly $3.1B acquisition; DBRG is no longer a public ticker.

questions.q: Which of these is part of the plate, not a cake layer?
questions.why: The plate holds the cake up: capital, data, talent, policy, and materials.

questions.q: Why is circular financing a risk to read in AI revenue?
options: Some revenue at one layer is funded by investment from another, overstating independent demand
questions.why: When a chipmaker invests in a customer who buys its chips, part of demand is self-financed.

questions.q: In mid-October 2026 CoreWeave's unsecured bonds yielded over 15% while the broad high-yield index spread stayed near 3.2 points. What does that gap most likely signal?
options: A broad credit crisis has begun
Lenders are repricing the weakest, most leveraged AI borrowers rather than all credit
questions.why: Stress concentrated in single names and CCC credits while the index stays tight is how late-cycle cracks usually start: the marginal borrower pays first.

questions.q: ASML said in October 2026 that its planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet customer demand. Why does that matter for the AI cake?
options: It means chip demand is falling
Lithography tools could become a second bottleneck alongside power, capping how fast new chip capacity arrives
questions.why: Every leading-edge wafer needs EUV tools. If ASML cannot ship enough, fab capacity, and so GPU supply, grows more slowly than demand.

questions.q: Meta guided 2026 capex to $130-145B and reported Q2 free cash flow of about $0.8B. If capex keeps rising, what is the most likely funding source?
options: Cutting the dividend to zero alone
More debt, leases, and off-balance-sheet partners like the Blue Owl Hyperion JV
questions.why: When operating cash no longer covers capex, the gap is filled with borrowing and partner capital. That shifts risk from shareholders to lenders.

questions.q: Google's October 2026 deal with Constellation adds new nuclear power mainly by which method?
options: Uprating existing reactors to produce more power
questions.why: Uprates at 11 existing units (890 MW under a 20-year PPA) are faster and cheaper than new builds, which is why they come first.

questions.q: If CoreWeave needs to refinance unsecured debt while its bonds yield over 15%, which outcome is most consistent with the cycle model?
options: Growth funded by secured, contract-backed or customer-prepaid debt instead, with slower expansion if that is not enough
questions.why: High unsecured costs push neoclouds toward asset-backed and prepaid financing. If those channels tighten too, capacity growth slows, an early overbuild-to-digestion signal.
